terminal.description: A shell in your workspace where each part of the order screen watches only what it shows, and prints when it is drawn again.

tasks.title: Watch one part
tasks.description:
Implement `watch(store, selector, listener)` in `src/store.js`.

- `selector` is a function that picks a part out of the state, such as `(state) => state.basket.length`
- `watch` reads the part once when it is called; after each change of the state, it picks the part again and tells `listener(part, previousPart)` only when the part changed
- parts are compared with `Object.is`: a number or a text worked out again is the same when its value is; a new array or object is always a change
- `watch` returns a function that stops it

The check watches numbers, texts, arrays and `NaN` with selectors of its own, makes changes that do and do not touch them, and notes every call.
nextSteps: Run `node src/try.js` and read the error.
Build `watch` on `store.subscribe`: it is a listener that compares before it passes the news on.
Keep the part from the last time in a variable, starting with the part when `watch` is called.
hints: A part of the screen does not care about the whole state, only about its piece of it. `watch` stands between the store and that part, and keeps quiet when its piece did not change.
Inside the listener you give `subscribe`, run the selector on the new state and compare the result with the one you kept. When they differ, keep the new one and tell the listener.

`let current = selector(store.getState())`, then `return store.subscribe((state) => { const next = selector(state); if (Object.is(current, next)) return; const previous = current; current = next; listener(next, previous) })`.

tasks.title: Decide what counts as a change
tasks.description:
Give `watch` a fourth argument, `isEqual`, for parts that are made new every time.

- `watch(store, selector, listener, isEqual)`: when `isEqual` is given, `isEqual(previousPart, part)` decides alone, in place of `Object.is`; `true` means the part did not change
- it is called once per round, with the part before first and the new part second
- when it says the part changed, the listener is told with the new part and the part before, as in task 1
- without `isEqual`, parts are still compared with `Object.is`

The check watches a part made new on every round, `{ jobs, ink }`, with and without an `isEqual` of its own, and with one that never calls two parts the same.
nextSteps: Run `node src/try.js`: the summary line passes `shallowEqual` as a fourth argument, which is the next task.
Where you compare with `Object.is`, use `isEqual` when it is given.
hints: A selector that returns `{ jobs, ink }` makes a new object every time it runs, so `Object.is` calls every round a change. Only whoever wrote the selector knows what "the same" means for it.
A default parameter, `isEqual = Object.is`, gives you one name for both cases.
`export function watch(store, selector, listener, isEqual = Object.is)`, and `if (isEqual(current, next)) return` in place of the `Object.is` check.

tasks.title: Compare an object key by key
tasks.description:
Implement `shallowEqual(a, b)` in `src/store.js`, a ready-made `isEqual` for parts that are small objects.

- it is `true` when `Object.is(a, b)` is
- otherwise both have to be objects, not `null`, with the same keys, in any order, and each key's values the same by `Object.is`; arrays count, by their places
- it looks one level deep only: two values that are each their own array or object are different, whatever is inside them
- in every other case it is `false`

The check calls `shallowEqual` with pairs of its own, then uses it with `watch` on a part made new every round.
nextSteps: Read "One level down" in the lesson.
Start with the easy answers: the same value, then two values that are not both objects.
Compare the number of keys, then every key of the first with the same key of the second.
hints: `shallowEqual` answers one question: would a part made of these values look the same on screen? It looks at each value once, never inside it.
`Object.keys(a)` gives the keys. A key the second object lacks reads as `undefined` there, the same as a key that holds `undefined`, so ask `Object.hasOwn(b, key)` too.

After `if (Object.is(a, b)) return true` and the object check, `const keys = Object.keys(a)`, then `keys.length === Object.keys(b).length && keys.every((key) => Object.hasOwn(b, key) && Object.is(a[key], b[key]))`.
